To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of a custom-made femoral stem that is shorter and more proximal than conventional femoral implants, in combination with a specific surgical technique, is associated with an increase in periprosthetic DXAs in the proximal femur.
Progressive shortening of the length of the femoral component in THA produces more proximal bone loading, which preserves metaphyseally bone and increases BMD in medial ROIs over the time.
progressive shortening and distal unloading of the stem of femoral components of THA effectively preserve metaphyseal BMD and increase periprosthetic DXB in medial ROIs over the time.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and validation of a novel DXA protocol of analysis for periprosthetic evaluation, and with the assessment of the effect of progressive stem shortening on bone remodeling after cementless primary THA.
the evaluation of bone response to new implant designs.
the evaluation of the biological effects of a new concept in the design of femoral stems, which is based on the use of short and ultra-short stems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the type 2 implant was associated with better preservation of periprostheic bone density, particularly in the most distal regions of the femur, compared to the type 1 implant.
the new implant design with the shortest stem and the highest degree of proximal loading is the best in terms of periprosthetics bone remodeling, but the differences are not clinically significant.
the use of short femoral stems in THA is a safe and efficient strategy to preserve bone stock and to improve the biological response of the periprosthetic environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more proximal loading of the femur, the more proximal the bone remodeling, which is a good thing.
DXA is a useful tool for the analysis of periprostheses with new designs and surgical techniques.
progressive shortening and distalization of the stem, which effectively preserves the bone of the metaphysis, can be used to improve the biological behavior of cementless femoral components.
The main takeaway from our work is that
shortening of the implant stem, with the consequent increase of the load transferred to the metaphyseal regions of interest, is a promising strategy to preserve bone stock after THA.
DXA can be used as a tool for assessing the biological response of the periprosthetic region to changes in implant design.
DXA can be used to evaluate the effect on periprostheic bone remodeling of the progressive shortening of femoral stems.
